result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.enumerate_all_cliques()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} List every clique of an undirected graph, smallest first. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L22436-L22488){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.enumerate_all_cliques() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Enumerate all cliques](/assets/graphs/enumerate-all-cliques.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Left: a triangle of nodes 1, 2, 3. Right: its seven cliques as miniature triangles in rows by size, each clique in the accent color: the three single nodes [1], [2], [3], the three edges [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], and the whole triangle [1, 2, 3]." width="100%"} Unlike `find_cliques()`, which reports only maximal cliques, this lists all of them: every single node, every edge, every triangle, and so on, ordered by size. Counting cliques of each size gives the clique profile used in network comparison, motif-style statistics and topological data analysis (the cliques are the simplices of the clique complex). The number of cliques can be exponential in the size of the largest one, so use it on sparse or small graphs. Parallel edges count once and self-loops are ignored. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The cliques as lists of node IDs, in non-decreasing order of size. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} A breadth-first expansion: each clique is extended only by common neighbors with a larger ID than its last node, so every clique is produced exactly once, in the same order as NetworkX's `enumerate_all_cliques`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A triangle has 7 cliques: three nodes, three edges and the triangle itself: ::: {#d372b5dd .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec triangle = ec.Graph().add_cycle_graph(3) triangle.enumerate_all_cliques() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [[1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3]] ``` ::: :::
